## How to Control Ejaculation With Your Pelvic Floor
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-to-control-ejaculation/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

Learning how to control ejaculation with pelvic floor muscles is mostly about timing: noticing arousal early, easing off before the point of no return, and keeping the pelvic floor relaxed rather than clenched. Strength helps, but awareness and the ability to let go matter just as much.

> **Short answer:** Train your pelvic floor to both squeeze and fully relax, use an arousal scale to slow down at about 6–7 out of 10, and practice with slow breathing. Studies suggest pelvic floor training may help some men, but it is not a guaranteed fix.

## Why the Pelvic Floor Affects Ejaculation

Ejaculation happens in two phases. In the **emission** phase, semen moves into the urethra. In the **expulsion** phase, pelvic floor muscles, especially the bulbospongiosus, contract rhythmically to push it out.

The pelvic floor is the part of this reflex you can train voluntarily, and better control of it may help some men delay ejaculation. In a [small 2014 study by Pastore and colleagues](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4003840/), most men with lifelong premature ejaculation gained some control after a 12-week supervised rehabilitation program. That program included biofeedback and electrical stimulation, not just home Kegels. See [Do Kegels Help With Premature Ejaculation?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/do-kegels-help-premature-ejaculation/).

## The Point of No Return

Once emission starts, ejaculation follows within seconds and is very hard to stop. That moment is the "point of no return." Every control technique works **before** it, not at it. That is why squeezing hard at the last second rarely works.

## Use an Arousal Scale

Rate arousal from 0 to 10, where 10 is ejaculation:

| Level | What it feels like | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0–3 | Calm to mild arousal | Keep going |
| 4–6 | Clear arousal, steady breathing | Notice your body, stay relaxed |
| 7 | Strong arousal, breathing speeds up | Slow down or pause |
| 8–9 | Close to the edge | Stop completely; it may already be too late |
| 10 | Ejaculation | — |

The skill is catching 6–7 reliably. Many men only notice 9 at first, so practice paying attention earlier.

## Squeeze or Relax? Using Your Pelvic Floor in the Moment

- **Relaxing** is the default. Tension in the pelvic floor, buttocks, thighs and belly tends to push arousal higher. When you reach 6–7, exhale and consciously soften the pelvic floor, as in a [reverse Kegel](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/).
- **A gentle squeeze** is a tool some men use as a cue: one or two light contractions at 6–7, combined with slowing down, then a full release.

If squeezing makes you feel more tense or closer to the edge, skip it and rely on relaxation. A [2023 study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414676/) that added sphincter control training, which focuses on awareness and relaxation of the pelvic sphincters, to the stop-start technique reported better results than stop-start alone, though it was not randomized. For a full comparison, read [Kegel vs Reverse Kegel for Premature Ejaculation](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegel-vs-reverse-kegel-premature-ejaculation/).

## Breathing: The Simplest Lever

Fast breathing and breath-holding usually come with rising arousal. Slow breathing helps you stay mid-scale.

- Inhale through the nose for about 4 seconds, letting the belly expand.
- Exhale for about 6 seconds and let the pelvic floor soften.
- Keep the jaw and shoulders loose.

## How to Control Ejaculation Mentally

Thinking of something unsexy often backfires, because you stop noticing your arousal. Instead:

- Stay present and track sensations, so you notice 6–7 in time.
- Reduce performance anxiety. Anxiety speeds things up for many men.
- Talk with your partner, so pausing feels normal rather than awkward.

If anxiety, relationship stress or past experiences play a big role, a sex therapist can help.

## How to Control Ejaculation Naturally: A 4-Week Practice Plan

This is a general practice structure, not a clinical protocol.

| Week | Pelvic floor training (most days) | Arousal practice (2–3 times a week) |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Find the muscles; short squeezes and full relaxation, a few minutes a day | Solo: rate arousal, no pauses needed |
| 2 | Add holds of a few seconds and quick squeezes; equal rest | Solo [stop-start](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/stop-start-technique/): pause at 7, 3–4 rounds |
| 3 | Add relaxation breathing after each set | Solo: pause at 6–7 using breathing and a soft release |
| 4 | Keep the routine; avoid adding many extra reps | With a partner: agreed pause signal, slow movement |

If you are unsure which muscles to use, start with [How to Find Your Pelvic Floor Muscles](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/). Stop and get assessed if training causes pain, urinary symptoms or a constant clenched feeling.

## When to See a Doctor

See a urologist or sexual medicine clinician if premature ejaculation is new, happens with erection problems, pain or urinary symptoms, or affects your relationship or wellbeing. [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/premature-ejaculation/diagnosis-treatment/drc-20354905) lists behavioral techniques, pelvic floor exercises, counseling and medication among treatment options.

## Guided Timing for Squeeze and Release

Kegel Morse Hero turns pelvic floor training into Morse-code rhythms: a dot is a quick squeeze, a dash is a longer hold, and the gaps are full relaxation, with haptic cues so you can train discreetly. That makes it easier to practice both the squeeze and the release you need for control. It guides timing only; it does not measure muscle activity or treat premature ejaculation.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can you control ejaculation with pelvic floor muscles?

Some men can learn more control by training awareness, contraction and relaxation of the pelvic floor. Small studies suggest pelvic floor rehabilitation may help men with premature ejaculation, but results vary and protocols differ.

### How to control ejaculation to last longer?

Combine an arousal scale, pausing at 6–7, slow breathing and a relaxed pelvic floor. Practice alone first, then with a partner.

### Should I squeeze or relax to stop ejaculating?

Relaxing is usually the better default. A short, gentle squeeze can work as a cue for some men, but a hard clench at the last second rarely stops ejaculation.

### How long does it take to learn ejaculation control?

Many men need several weeks of regular practice. The supervised program in the best-known study lasted 12 weeks.

## Kegel vs Reverse Kegel for Premature Ejaculation
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegel-vs-reverse-kegel-premature-ejaculation/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

In the Kegel vs reverse Kegel for premature ejaculation debate, the honest answer is that you usually need both: Kegels train contraction and control, while reverse Kegels train release. Regular Kegels have a small body of research in premature ejaculation; reverse Kegels have almost none directly, though relaxation is a recognized part of pelvic floor therapy.

> **Short answer:** If your pelvic floor feels weak or hard to find, start with Kegels plus full relaxation. If it feels tight, painful or constantly clenched, start with relaxation and reverse Kegels, and get assessed. Neither is a guaranteed fix for PE.

## What Is the Difference?

A **Kegel** is a voluntary contraction of the pelvic floor: a lift and squeeze, as if stopping the flow of urine or holding in gas. A **reverse Kegel** is the opposite movement: a deliberate, gentle release and lengthening of the pelvic floor, usually paired with a slow inhale. It is not straining or pushing as if on the toilet.

For a step-by-step guide to the release, read [Reverse Kegels for Men](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/). If you cannot find the muscles at all, start with [How to Find Your Pelvic Floor Muscles](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/).

## Kegel vs Reverse Kegel: Comparison Table

| | Kegel | Reverse Kegel |
|---|---|---|
| Movement | Lift and squeeze | Soften and lengthen |
| Breathing | Usually on exhale | Usually on inhale |
| Main skill | Strength, endurance, voluntary control | Relaxation, coordination, letting go |
| Best fit | Weak or under-active pelvic floor | Tight, overactive or painful pelvic floor |
| Direct PE research | Small studies and reviews, mostly supervised programs | Very little direct research |
| Main risk | Overdoing it can add tension | Straining or bearing down if done wrong |
| Role during sex | Optional light squeeze as a cue | Release when arousal rises |

## What the Evidence Says About Kegels for Premature Ejaculation

Studies show that pelvic floor rehabilitation may help some men with premature ejaculation. In the [2014 study by Pastore and colleagues](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4003840/), most of the 40 men with lifelong PE gained some control after a 12-week program. But that program included biofeedback and electrical stimulation, not just home exercises.

A [2019 systematic review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30979506/) found pelvic floor training looked helpful for PE and erectile dysfunction, but protocols varied widely. A [2026 meta-analysis](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42132359/) was more cautious: pelvic floor and sphincter-control training showed a smaller effect on latency than the comparison treatments in the included studies. The full picture is in [Do Kegels Help With Premature Ejaculation?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/do-kegels-help-premature-ejaculation/).

## Does Reverse Kegel Help With Premature Ejaculation?

There are no good trials testing reverse Kegels alone for premature ejaculation. Claims that they are "the real cure" come from forums, not research.

The evidence that exists is indirect:

- A [2023 study](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10414676/) found that adding sphincter control training, which focuses on awareness and relaxation of the pelvic sphincters, to the stop-start technique worked better than stop-start alone. It was not randomized, and it is not identical to reverse Kegels.
- Relaxation-based pelvic floor therapy is used for men with pelvic pain and [ejaculation-related pain](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/35576002/).
- Tension tends to raise arousal, which is one reason relaxation is often taught as they approach the point of no return.

So reverse Kegels make sense as a relaxation skill, especially for a tight pelvic floor, but there is no evidence that they work better than Kegels for PE in general.

## Which Should You Start With? Weak vs Tight Pelvic Floor

Only an assessment can tell for sure, but these patterns are a rough guide.

**Signs your pelvic floor may be under-active (start with Kegels plus full release):**

- You struggle to feel or hold a contraction.
- You have dribbling after urinating or leaks with effort.

**Signs it may be overactive or tight (start with relaxation and reverse Kegels):**

- Pelvic, perineal or testicular pain, or pain after ejaculation.
- Difficulty starting urination or a weak stream.
- A constant clenched feeling, or symptoms that get worse after Kegels.

These symptoms can have other causes, so they are a reason to see a clinician, not a self-diagnosis. [Cleveland Clinic](https://my.clevelandclinic.org/health/diseases/22870-hypertonic-pelvic-floor) describes physical therapy as central to treating a diagnosed hypertonic pelvic floor.

## Reverse Kegel Exercises for Premature Ejaculation: A Balanced Routine

Without pain, a balanced session covers both directions:

1. **Release first:** 3–5 slow breaths, letting the pelvic floor soften on each inhale.
2. **Kegels:** a few short squeezes and a few longer holds, each followed by full relaxation at least as long as the squeeze.
3. **Release again:** 3–5 slow breaths to finish.
4. **Apply it:** during [stop-start practice](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/stop-start-technique/), use the release when arousal reaches 6–7.

Do not hold your breath or bear down. Stop if anything hurts. For in-the-moment technique, read [How to Control Ejaculation With Your Pelvic Floor](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-to-control-ejaculation/).

It guides timing only; it does not measure muscle tension, tell you whether your pelvic floor is weak or tight, or treat premature ejaculation.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does reverse Kegel help with premature ejaculation?

It may help some men, especially those with a tight or overactive pelvic floor, by teaching them to relax instead of clench. There is very little direct research on reverse Kegels for PE.

### Are Kegels or reverse Kegels better for premature ejaculation?

Neither has been shown to be better for everyone. Kegels have more research, mostly from supervised programs; reverse Kegels fit best when tension or pain is involved. Many men train both.

### Can Kegels make premature ejaculation worse?

Possibly, if your pelvic floor is already overactive. If symptoms worsen or you develop pain after Kegels, stop and get assessed.

### Do reverse Kegels help you last longer?

They may help indirectly by reducing tension as arousal rises. They are not proven to increase time to ejaculation on their own.

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. If you have premature ejaculation with pain, urinary symptoms or erection problems, see a urologist, sexual medicine clinician or pelvic floor physical therapist.*

## PC Muscle Exercises for Men: Find It and Train It
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/pc-muscle-exercises-for-men/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

PC muscle exercises for men are simply Kegels: you lift and squeeze the muscles you would use to stop urine and hold in gas, then fully let go. Find the right muscle first, train slow holds and quick squeezes a few times a day, and practice relaxing as carefully as you practice squeezing.

> **Short answer:** Locate the muscle with a "stop the stream" or "hold in gas" test, then do slow holds, quick squeezes and full relaxation daily for at least several weeks. A PC muscle trainer can add feedback, but it is optional.

## What Is the PC Muscle?

"PC" stands for pubococcygeus. It is one part of the levator ani, the muscle sheet that runs from the pubic bone at the front to the tailbone at the back and supports the bladder and bowel.

In everyday use, "PC muscle" usually means the whole pelvic floor you feel when you squeeze. That is fine for training, because you cannot contract the pubococcygeus on its own anyway. Two smaller muscles near the base of the penis, the bulbocavernosus and ischiocavernosus, matter most for erections and ejaculation, and they work together with the deeper layer during a normal Kegel.

## How to Find Your PC Muscle

Try these checks once or twice, not as daily exercises:

1. **Gas test.** Imagine you are in a quiet room and need to hold in gas. The squeeze-and-lift you feel around the back passage is the pelvic floor.
2. **Urine test.** Midway through peeing, slow or stop the stream once. Do not make this a routine, because repeatedly interrupting urination is not recommended.
3. **Mirror test.** Standing, tighten as if stopping urine and gas. The base of the penis should draw slightly in and the testicles should rise.
4. **Hand check.** Place two fingers on the skin between the scrotum and anus. You should feel a gentle lift inward, not a push outward.

If your buttocks clench, your belly hardens or you hold your breath, you are using the wrong muscles. Training through pelvic pain is also a reason to stop and get assessed. Our guide on [how to find your pelvic floor muscles](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/) covers more cues.

## 5 PC Muscle Exercises for Men

Start lying down with knees bent. It is the easiest position to feel the lift.

### 1. Slow holds (strength)

Squeeze and lift, hold for 3 to 5 seconds, then relax for the same time or longer. Build toward holds of up to about 10 seconds over several weeks. Stop the hold when form slips.

### 2. Quick squeezes (fast response)

Squeeze firmly for about one second, release completely, repeat 5 to 10 times. The difference between the two types is explained in [quick vs slow Kegels](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/quick-vs-slow-kegels/).

### 3. Half-strength lift (control)

Lift to roughly half of your maximum and hold it while breathing normally. In a well-known erectile dysfunction trial, men were asked to lift their pelvic floor about 50% while walking. This teaches control rather than maximal effort.

### 4. Functional squeeze (the habit)

Tighten just before you cough, sneeze or lift something heavy. After urinating, give one firm squeeze to clear the last drops.

### 5. Full relaxation drop (the reset)

After each set, let the pelvic floor drop and soften on a slow breath out. A tight, always-on pelvic floor can cause pain or urinary trouble, so relaxing is part of the exercise. See [reverse Kegels for men](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/) for a gentle version.

## How to Strengthen PC Muscles: A Weekly Plan

| Week | Position | Slow holds | Quick squeezes | Sessions per day |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1–2 | Lying | 5 × 3–5 s | 5 | 2 |
| 3–4 | Lying, sitting | 8 × 5–6 s | 8 | 2–3 |
| 5–8 | Sitting, standing | 10 × 6–8 s | 10 | 3 |
| 9+ | Standing, walking | 10 × up to 10 s | 10 | 3, plus functional squeezes |

Rest at least as long as you hold. Breathe throughout. If you want a sense of volume limits, read [how many Kegels a day for men](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-many-kegels-a-day-for-men/). Most official guidance says results take weeks to months, not days.

## Do PC Muscle Trainers Work?

A "PC muscle trainer" can mean three things:

- **Biofeedback devices.** Some, such as the kGoal Boost, are non-insertable pads you sit on that show how strongly you contract. Clinics use similar feedback; the best-known ED trial combined exercises with anal pressure biofeedback supervised by a physiotherapist. Feedback can help you learn the movement, but no device does the work for you.
- **Timer and guide apps.** They structure holds, rests and reminders. They do not measure anything.
- **Grippers, weights and "PC builders."** Be skeptical of products that promise size or dramatic results. Pelvic floor training is not shown to change penis size.

If you cannot feel any lift after a few weeks, a pelvic floor physical therapist is usually more useful than a gadget.

Ring animation and haptics guide each rep, so you can follow the timing eyes-free at 1x, 2x or 3x speed. It guides timing only; it does not measure your muscles or treat any condition.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do I strengthen my PC muscles fast?

There is no fast track. Consistent daily slow holds and quick squeezes with good form, progressed over weeks, beat high rep counts. Most men need several weeks before noticing a change.

### Are pubococcygeus muscle exercises for men different from Kegels?

No. Pubococcygeus exercises, PC muscle exercises and Kegels all train the same pelvic floor group.

### Do I need a PC muscle trainer?

No. A biofeedback device can help if you struggle to feel the muscle, but many men learn with body cues, a timer and, when needed, a physical therapist.

### What are the benefits of PC muscle exercises for men sexually?

Studies suggest pelvic floor training may help some men with erection firmness or ejaculatory control, especially in supervised programs. Results vary, and they are not guaranteed.

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. If you have pain, urinary symptoms or sexual concerns, see a urologist, sexual medicine clinician or pelvic floor physical therapist.*

## Pelvic Floor Exercises for Erectile Dysfunction: A Routine
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/pelvic-floor-exercises-for-erectile-dysfunction/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

Pelvic floor exercises for erectile dysfunction usually mean strong pelvic floor squeezes done lying, sitting and standing every morning and evening, plus light lifts while walking, kept up for about three months. The routine below is modeled on the best-known randomized trial of this approach. It may help some men, but it works best after a medical check and alongside other healthy changes.

> **Short answer:** Do 3 strong holds lying, 3 sitting and 3 standing, twice a day, add a gentle lift while walking and a squeeze after urinating, and review progress at 3 months. See a doctor first, because ED can be an early sign of heart disease.

## See a Doctor Before You Start

Erectile dysfunction is a symptom, not a diagnosis. [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/erectile-dysfunction/in-depth/erectile-dysfunction/art-20045141) explains that ED can be an early warning sign of heart disease, because the smaller arteries in the penis may show blood flow problems before heart symptoms appear.

[NIDDK](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/erectile-dysfunction/symptoms-causes) lists vascular disease, diabetes, hormone problems, nerve damage, medicines and psychological factors among the causes. A clinician can check blood pressure, blood sugar, cholesterol and hormones. Do not stop a prescribed medicine on your own; ask the prescriber to review it.

## What the Evidence Says, in One Paragraph

A small 2004 trial by Dorey and colleagues found that pelvic floor exercises with biofeedback and lifestyle advice improved erectile function more than lifestyle advice alone at three months. Later reviews are mixed, and one 2024 meta-analysis found clearer benefit from aerobic exercise than from pelvic floor training alone. We cover the details in [Can Kegels help erectile dysfunction?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegels-erectile-dysfunction/). This page is the practical side.

## Why Pelvic Floor Exercises May Help Erectile Function

Two muscles at the base of the penis, the ischiocavernosus and bulbocavernosus, contract during an erection. Their contraction raises pressure inside the penis, and the bulbocavernosus helps limit blood flowing back out. That is the idea behind pelvic floor exercises for erectile function. Blood vessels, nerves and hormones still do most of the work, so exercises are an add-on, not a replacement for care.

## Pelvic Floor Exercises for Erectile Dysfunction: The Routine

In the Dorey trial, a physiotherapist taught each man individually over five weekly 30-minute sessions using biofeedback. At home, men did the exercises daily. The handout looked roughly like this:

| Position | How | Morning | Evening |
|---|---|---|---|
| Standing | Feet apart; tighten as if stopping urine and gas. Base of the penis draws in, testicles rise. | 3 strong holds | 3 strong holds |
| Sitting | Knees apart; lift the pelvic floor without lifting your buttocks off the chair. | 3 strong holds | 3 strong holds |
| Lying | On your back, knees bent and apart; tighten and lift. | 3 strong holds | 3 strong holds |
| Walking | Lift to about half of your maximum now and then. | During the day | During the day |
| After urinating | One strong squeeze to clear the last drops. | Each time | Each time |

That is 18 strong contractions a day. In the trial, hold length was set individually by the physiotherapist. At home, a sensible approach is to hold only as long as you can keep good form, often 3 to 5 seconds at first, and build toward about 10 seconds. Rest at least as long as you held.

The handout also suggested rhythmic pelvic floor tightening during sexual activity to help maintain rigidity. Treat that as optional practice once the basic squeeze feels easy.

## Your 12-Week Plan

1. **Weeks 1–2: learn.** Start lying down. Find the lift, keep breathing, relax fully between holds. Our guide on [finding your pelvic floor muscles](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-to-find-pelvic-floor-muscles-men/) helps here.
2. **Weeks 3–6: full routine.** Add sitting and standing, twice daily, 3 holds per position.
3. **Weeks 7–12: build.** Lengthen the holds, add the walking lift and the post-urination squeeze.
4. **Week 12: review.** In the trial, outcomes were measured at 3 months, and men kept exercising toward 6 months.

Read [how long Kegels take to work for men](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-long-do-kegels-take-to-work-for-men/) for realistic timelines.

## Pair It With Lifestyle Changes

Men in the trial also got advice on smoking, alcohol, general fitness, healthy diet, weight and saddle pressure from cycling. A 2024 meta-analysis found aerobic exercise improved erectile function, so brisk walking, cycling or swimming several times a week is a strong partner to the routine.

## When to Stop or Change Course

Stop strengthening and get assessed if you notice pelvic pain, pain after ejaculation, a weak or hesitant urine stream, or symptoms that get worse after exercising. These can point to an overactive pelvic floor, which needs relaxation work rather than more squeezing. See [reverse Kegels for men](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/).

## Follow the Routine With Kegel Morse Hero

Kegel Morse Hero guides squeeze-and-rest timing with Morse-code rhythms: dashes for longer holds, dots for quick squeezes and gaps for full relaxation, with haptics so you can train discreetly morning and evening. Reminders and session history help you stay consistent for the full 12 weeks. It does not measure muscle activity, diagnose ED or treat it.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Do pelvic floor exercises for erectile function really work?

Studies show they may help some men, especially in supervised programs with biofeedback. Evidence is mixed overall, and results are not guaranteed.

### Is there a Kegel exercises for erectile dysfunction physiotherapy guide I can follow?

The routine above follows the published Dorey trial handout. A pelvic floor physical therapist can tailor hold times and check your technique, which home routines cannot do.

### Do Kegels help with erectile strength?

They may help rigidity for some men because the muscles at the base of the penis support erections. Blood flow, nerves and hormones matter more, so a medical check comes first.

### Can Kegel exercises cause erectile dysfunction?

There is no good evidence that normal Kegels cause ED. Overdoing them, or training a pelvic floor that is already too tight, can cause pain or discomfort. See [can you do too many Kegels?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/can-you-do-too-many-kegels/).

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. For erectile problems, see your doctor, a urologist, sexual medicine clinician or pelvic floor physical therapist.*

## Death Grip Syndrome: Can You Get Sensitivity Back?
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/death-grip-syndrome/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

Death grip syndrome is an informal name for a pattern where a man gets used to a very tight, fast masturbation technique and then finds partnered sex does not feel strong enough to stay aroused or finish. Many men report that sensation and responsiveness improve after weeks of lighter, more varied stimulation, but research on it is very limited.

> **Short answer:** Death grip syndrome is not an official diagnosis, and it has barely been studied. Retraining with a lighter grip, lube, variety and short breaks is low-risk and worth trying, but numbness or orgasm problems in every situation need a medical check.

## What Is Death Grip Syndrome?

The term comes from online forums and sex educators, not from medical textbooks. It describes:

- Masturbating with a firm grip, high speed or one very specific technique.
- Finding that a partner's touch, oral sex or intercourse feels "too soft."
- Losing an erection or being unable to ejaculate during partnered sex, while solo sex works fine.

The key feature is that the problem is **situational**. If you can still reach orgasm with your usual technique, your nerves are likely working. The issue is what your body has learned to expect.

## What Does the Research Say About Death Grip Syndrome?

Honestly, very little. There are no large studies measuring "death grip" as a condition, and you will not find it in major urology guidelines.

What does exist is clinical literature on **delayed ejaculation**, where some sex therapists describe idiosyncratic masturbation habits, meaning a technique that a partner cannot easily reproduce, as one possible contributor. The [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/ejaculation-problems/) lists psychological causes, medicines and conditions like diabetes for delayed ejaculation, and names sex therapy with structured changes to your sex life as a treatment. Death grip retraining fits within that behavioral approach.

So the reasonable conclusion is: the habit-based explanation is plausible, the retraining advice is low-risk, and there is no proof of how long recovery takes or how many men it helps.

## How to Retrain: A 4-Week Plan

This plan is about changing what your body is used to. Go at your own pace.

| Week | Focus | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Pause | Take 5–7 days off masturbation and porn if you can. Not as punishment, just a reset. |
| 2 | Lighter grip | Use lube and a loose grip, roughly the pressure a partner would use. Go slower. Stop before switching back to your old technique. |
| 3 | Variety | Change hand, position, speed and type of touch. Try finishing with lighter stimulation even if it takes longer. |
| 4 | Bring it to partnered sex | More foreplay, less pressure to finish, open talk with your partner about what works. |

### Practical tips that help

- **Lube every time.** It reduces friction and makes lighter touch feel like enough.
- **Less intense content.** If you rely on very specific or extreme content, arousal during real sex may feel flat by comparison. Reducing it is part of the reset.
- **Mindful attention.** Focus on what you physically feel instead of chasing the finish. This is the core of sensate focus exercises used in sex therapy.
- **Do not judge one night.** Progress is uneven. Look at the trend over weeks.

## Can Pelvic Floor Training Help?

Not directly. Kegels do not make nerves more sensitive. They may help indirectly: firmer erections, more awareness of arousal and better control can make partnered sex feel more intense. If you tend to clench during sex, learning to fully relax the pelvic floor is just as important as squeezing. Read more in [Feel Less During Sex?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/increase-male-sensitivity/) and our guide to [reverse Kegels](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/reverse-kegels-for-men/).

Some men also ask whether edging or abstinence changes hormones. There is no good evidence that a short break or occasional edging meaningfully raises or lowers testosterone; see [Edging and Testosterone](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/edging-and-testosterone/).

## When It Is Something Else

Death grip is a convenient explanation, but it should not hide a medical problem. Consider other causes if:

- **Erections fail in every situation**, including solo. That points toward [erectile dysfunction](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegels-erectile-dysfunction/), which can be linked to heart, blood-vessel, hormone and medication factors.
- **Orgasm is delayed or absent even with your usual technique.** This may be delayed ejaculation. The [AUA/SMSNA guideline](https://www.auanet.org/guidelines-and-quality/guidelines/disorders-of-ejaculation) covers its assessment.
- **You take antidepressants**, especially SSRIs, or other medicines such as some blood pressure drugs or antipsychotics. These can dull sensation and delay orgasm. Do not stop them on your own; ask the prescriber.
- **You have numbness or tingling**, especially with diabetes, back problems, long cycling or numbness elsewhere. This may be a nerve issue.
- **You have low desire, fatigue and weaker erections together**, which can suggest low testosterone.

See a doctor soon for sudden genital numbness, and urgently if it comes with leg weakness or loss of bladder or bowel control.

## Use Guided Timing for Squeezes and Full Relaxation

If you add pelvic floor work to your plan, Kegel Morse Hero guides the timing with Morse-code rhythms: quick squeezes for dots, longer holds for dashes and full relaxation in the gaps, with haptics so you can train discreetly. It does not measure muscle activity or treat death grip, ED or delayed ejaculation.

[Explore Kegel Morse Hero on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kegel-morse-hero-pelvic-floor/id6761460873)

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Is death grip syndrome real?

It is not a medical diagnosis, and research is very limited. The pattern many men describe, where partner sex feels too soft after years of tight-grip masturbation, is plausible and overlaps with what clinicians see in delayed ejaculation.

### How long does death grip syndrome recovery take?

There is no reliable data. Many men describe changes over a few weeks to a few months of consistent retraining, but this varies a lot and is not guaranteed.

### Is death grip syndrome permanent?

There is no evidence that a tight grip causes permanent nerve damage. If numbness persists despite retraining, look for a medical cause.

### Can I fix death grip without stopping masturbation?

Many men simply change technique: lube, a lighter grip, slower pace and more variety. A short break can make the change easier, but it is not required.

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. If symptoms persist, see a urologist, sexual medicine clinician or pelvic floor physical therapist for personal guidance.*

## Do Kegels Help Sexual Stamina? An Honest Answer
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/do-kegels-help-sexual-stamina/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

Do Kegels help sexual stamina? Partly. Studies suggest pelvic floor training may help some men with ejaculatory control and erection firmness, two things people often mean by stamina. Kegels do not improve your heart and lung fitness, your energy or your desire, so they cover only one piece of the picture.

> **Short answer:** Kegels may help you last longer and keep a firmer erection, especially in supervised programs, but results vary. For overall stamina in bed, pair them with regular aerobic exercise and get persistent problems checked.

## Do Kegels Help Sexual Stamina? It Depends on What You Mean

The word covers several different things, and Kegels affect them differently:

| What people mean | Main drivers | Can Kegels help? |
|---|---|---|
| Lasting longer before ejaculation | Arousal level, nervous system, pelvic floor control, anxiety | May help some men |
| Keeping a firm erection | Blood vessels, nerves, hormones, pelvic floor muscles | May help some men |
| Not getting tired or out of breath | Heart and lung fitness, sleep, weight | No, that is aerobic fitness |
| Wanting sex and having energy | Hormones, mood, sleep, relationship, medicines | Not directly |

Separating these helps you pick the right tool instead of expecting one exercise to fix everything.

## Kegels and Lasting Longer

In a 2014 study by Pastore and colleagues, 40 men with lifelong premature ejaculation completed a 12-week pelvic floor rehabilitation program, and 33 gained control over the ejaculatory reflex by the end. The program included physiotherapy, biofeedback and electrical stimulation, so it was more than home Kegels, and the study was small.

A 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis was more cautious: pelvic floor training showed a smaller effect on measured latency than some comparison treatments. The fair summary is that it may help, but it is not a guaranteed method. Our article on [Kegels and premature ejaculation](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/do-kegels-help-premature-ejaculation/) has the details, and the [stop-start technique](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/stop-start-technique/) is a well-known behavioral method that pairs naturally with pelvic floor work.

## Kegels and Erection Firmness

The muscles at the base of the penis contract during an erection and help maintain rigidity. In a 2004 trial of 55 men with erectile dysfunction, pelvic floor exercises with biofeedback and lifestyle advice improved erectile function more than advice alone at three months. However, a 2024 meta-analysis found no significant improvement in its pelvic floor training subgroup, while aerobic exercise did help. See [Kegels for erectile dysfunction](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegels-erectile-dysfunction/) for the evidence.

## Do Kegels Help Sexual Performance in Other Ways?

Some men report better awareness of their pelvic floor, which can make it easier to notice rising tension and relax it. That is a reasonable mechanism, but it is not well measured. Kegels are not shown to increase penis size, raise testosterone or boost libido. For those questions, read [can Kegels increase libido or testosterone?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/can-kegels-increase-libido-testosterone/).

## The Role of Aerobic Fitness

If you get winded, tired or lose your erection as sex goes on, cardio fitness is likely the bigger lever. Erections depend on healthy blood vessels, and the 2024 meta-analysis found aerobic exercise improved erectile function. Regular walking, cycling, running or swimming also improves endurance, sleep and mood, all of which feed into stamina.

## Kegel Exercises for Sexual Stamina: A Simple Plan

1. **Pelvic floor, daily (5 minutes).** Slow holds, quick squeezes and full relaxation, twice a day. Start with our [Kegel exercises to last longer in bed](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegel-exercises-to-last-longer-in-bed/) plan.
2. **Relaxation, every set.** Let the pelvic floor fully drop after each squeeze. A constantly tight pelvic floor can make early ejaculation or pain worse.
3. **Aerobic exercise, most days.** Aim for regular moderate cardio you can keep up.
4. **Behavioral practice.** Try the stop-start technique alone or with a partner.
5. **Basics.** Sleep, less alcohol, no smoking.
6. **Review at 8 to 12 weeks.** Pelvic floor changes take weeks, not days.

## When to See a Doctor

Get checked if erection problems are new or worsening, if early ejaculation started after years of normal control, or if you have pain, urinary symptoms or low desire. ED can share causes with heart disease and diabetes, and [NIDDK](https://www.niddk.nih.gov/health-information/urologic-diseases/erectile-dysfunction/symptoms-causes) lists medicines and hormone problems among other causes.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What are the best Kegel exercises for sexual stamina?

A mix of slow holds for strength, quick squeezes for fast control and full relaxation between reps. Relaxation matters as much as squeezing for lasting longer.

### Do Kegels help sexual performance?

They may help some men with ejaculatory control and erection firmness. They do not improve cardio fitness, desire or size.

### Do Kegels make you last longer?

Small studies suggest pelvic floor rehabilitation may help some men with premature ejaculation, mostly in supervised programs over about 12 weeks. Results vary.

### How long until Kegels improve stamina?

Expect several weeks to a few months of consistent practice. Studies of pelvic floor programs for sexual function typically ran around three months.

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. For ongoing problems with erections or ejaculation, see a urologist, sexual medicine clinician or pelvic floor physical therapist.*

## Can Kegels Increase Libido or Testosterone?
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/can-kegels-increase-libido-testosterone/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

Can Kegels increase libido? There is no good evidence that Kegel exercises directly raise sex drive or testosterone. They are small muscle exercises for the pelvic floor, not a hormonal workout. They may still help your sex life indirectly through erection quality, control and confidence.

> **Short answer:** No study shows that Kegels raise testosterone or libido directly. Sleep, weight, alcohol, stress, medicines, relationship factors and medical conditions matter far more. Kegels may help some men feel more confident and in control in bed.

## Can Kegels Increase Testosterone?

Testosterone is made mainly in the testicles, under signals from the brain. Large-muscle exercise such as strength training places a different kind of load on the body than a few seconds of pelvic floor squeezing. We found no clinical trial showing that pelvic floor training changes testosterone levels.

You may see claims that Kegels "boost T" because they increase blood flow to the pelvis. That is a guess dressed up as a fact. Blood flow and hormone production are different things.

If you suspect low testosterone, the answer is a blood test, not more reps. [Mayo Clinic](https://www.mayoclinic.org/diseases-conditions/male-hypogonadism/symptoms-causes/syc-20354881) lists symptoms of male hypogonadism such as low sex drive, erectile problems, fatigue and loss of muscle mass. A diagnosis needs symptoms plus properly timed blood tests.

## Do Kegels Increase Sex Drive?

Libido is mostly driven by the brain, hormones, mood and context. Kegels do not act on those directly, and no good study shows a direct libido effect.

There is one realistic indirect route: if sex has been frustrating because of weak erections or finishing too fast, and pelvic floor training helps with that, you may feel more interested in sex. That is a confidence effect, not a hormonal one.

## What Actually Affects Libido and Testosterone

| Factor | What we know | Practical step |
|---|---|---|
| Sleep | A small JAMA study found that one week of restricted sleep lowered daytime testosterone in young healthy men | Aim for consistent 7–9 hours |
| Body weight | Excess weight is linked with lower testosterone | Gradual weight loss with diet and exercise |
| Alcohol | The NHS lists heavy drinking as a cause of low sex drive | Cut back and notice the difference |
| Stress, anxiety, depression | Commonly reduce desire | Address the cause; consider professional support |
| Medicines | Some antidepressants and blood pressure medicines can lower libido | Ask the prescriber; do not stop on your own |
| Relationship | Conflict, routine and poor communication reduce desire | Talk openly; couples or sex therapy can help |
| Medical conditions | Diabetes, heart disease, underactive thyroid, hypogonadism | Get checked by a clinician |

The [NHS](https://www.nhs.uk/conditions/loss-of-libido/) covers most of these causes of low sex drive. Regular aerobic and strength exercise also supports cardiovascular health, weight and mood, which is a better bet for your sex life than any single exercise.

## Where Kegels May Help Indirectly

Kegels are not useless for sex. Their likely benefits are mechanical and behavioral:

1. **Erection quality.** The pelvic floor muscles help maintain rigidity. A [2004 randomized trial](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1324914/) found that pelvic floor exercises with biofeedback and lifestyle advice improved erectile function more than lifestyle advice alone. Newer reviews are mixed; see [Kegels and erectile dysfunction](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegels-erectile-dysfunction/).
2. **Ejaculation control.** A [2019 systematic review](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30979506/) concluded pelvic floor training appeared helpful for ED and premature ejaculation, but protocols varied widely. More in [Do Kegels Help Premature Ejaculation?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/do-kegels-help-premature-ejaculation/)
3. **Body awareness and confidence.** Knowing how to contract and fully relax these muscles can make you feel more in control, which can make sex feel less stressful.

What Kegels will not do: raise hormones, grow the penis or replace medical care for low testosterone. For the broader picture, read [What Do Kegels Do for Men?](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/what-do-kegels-do-for-men/)

## A Simple Starting Routine

If you want to try pelvic floor training for erection quality or control:

1. Find the muscles by imagining stopping urine and holding in gas at the same time.
2. Squeeze for 3 seconds, then relax fully for 5–6 seconds.
3. Do 10 reps, once or twice a day.
4. Add a few quick 1-second squeezes with full relaxation between them.
5. Give it 6–12 weeks before judging results.

Stop and get assessed if you develop pelvic pain, pain after ejaculation or difficulty starting urine. An over-tight pelvic floor needs relaxation, not more squeezing. See [How Many Kegels a Day for Men](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/how-many-kegels-a-day-for-men/) for volume.

## Use Guided Timing Without the Hype

Kegel Morse Hero guides pelvic floor timing with Morse-code rhythms: dots for quick squeezes, dashes for longer holds and gaps for full relaxation, with haptic cues for discreet training. It does not measure muscles, raise testosterone or treat any condition. It simply makes a consistent routine easier to follow.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Can Kegels increase libido?

Not directly. No good evidence shows Kegels raise sex drive. They may help indirectly if better erections or control make sex less stressful.

### Can Kegels increase testosterone?

There is no evidence that Kegels raise testosterone. If you have low desire, fatigue and weaker erections together, ask a clinician about a testosterone blood test.

### What do Kegels do for men sexually?

They may help some men with erection firmness and ejaculation control. Results vary, and they work best as part of a broader plan.

### What raises libido naturally?

Enough sleep, less alcohol, managing stress, regular exercise, a healthy weight and a good relationship with your partner are the most practical starting points.

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. For low desire or suspected low testosterone, see a doctor, urologist or sexual medicine clinician; for pelvic floor symptoms, see a pelvic floor physical therapist.*

## Less Feeling During Sex After a Baby? What Helps
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/less-feeling-during-sex-after-baby/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

Less feeling during sex after a baby is common and usually improves. Stretched or weakened pelvic floor muscles, healing tears, hormone-related vaginal dryness while breastfeeding, exhaustion and low mood can all dull sensation and arousal. Pelvic floor physiotherapy, gentle Kegels once you are cleared, lubrication and time help many women.

> **Short answer:** Reduced sensation after birth often comes from a combination of a weaker pelvic floor, healing tissue, dryness and fatigue. Get checked at your postnatal appointment, ask for pelvic floor physiotherapy, and see a doctor sooner if sex is painful or you notice bulging or heaviness.

## Why You Might Feel Less During Sex After a Baby

There is rarely one cause. Most women have a mix of the following.

### Pelvic floor stretch and weakness

Pregnancy and vaginal birth stretch the pelvic floor, the muscles that surround the vagina, urethra and anus. These muscles contribute to grip, arousal and the contractions of orgasm. When they are weak or hard to feel, the vagina can feel looser and sensations duller. A C-section does not fully protect the pelvic floor, because pregnancy itself loads it for months.

### Perineal tears, stitches and scar tissue

Tears and episiotomy scars can leave areas that feel numb, tight or tender while nerves and tissue recover, which makes it hard to relax and enjoy sex.

### Breastfeeding-related vaginal dryness

After birth, and especially while breastfeeding, estrogen levels stay low. The NHS notes that hormonal changes after birth can make the vagina drier than usual, and lists breastfeeding as a cause of vaginal dryness. Dryness causes friction and discomfort, which can numb pleasure even when the muscles are fine.

### Fatigue, mood and body changes

Broken sleep, the mental load of a newborn, touch fatigue and body-image changes all reduce desire and arousal. Low arousal means less lubrication and blood flow, so sensation drops. Postnatal depression and anxiety can also flatten pleasure and deserve care in their own right.

## No Sensation During Sex After Baby: Is It Normal?

Feeling "nothing" in the first weeks or months is something many new parents describe, and for most it improves as tissue heals, hormones settle and sleep returns. It is still worth raising at your postnatal check around 6–8 weeks, especially if it is not improving by several months after birth. You do not need to wait for a specific number of months to ask for help.

## What Helps: A Practical Plan

1. **Get the all-clear first.** Wait until bleeding has settled, stitches have healed and your midwife, doctor or postnatal check says activity is appropriate.
2. **Ask for pelvic floor physiotherapy.** A pelvic health physiotherapist can check whether your muscles are weak, tight or poorly coordinated, and tailor exercises. In some countries this is routine after birth; elsewhere you may need to ask.
3. **Start gentle Kegels once cleared.** Breathe out, gently close and lift around the vagina and anus, hold for a few comfortable seconds, then release fully. Build slowly. See [Kegels After Childbirth](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegels-after-childbirth/) for a first routine and [Kegel Exercises for Women](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegel-exercises-for-women/) for technique.
4. **Use lubricant generously.** A water-based or silicone-based lubricant reduces friction from dryness. Avoid perfumed products.
5. **Take more time for arousal.** Longer foreplay and non-penetrative touch let blood flow and natural lubrication build before penetration.
6. **Protect sleep and mood where you can.** Sharing night feeds, rest and support for low mood all feed back into desire and sensation.

## Do Kegels Help Sensation After Birth?

They may. A 2019 systematic review of 10 studies found that most reported improvements in desire, arousal, orgasm or satisfaction with postpartum pelvic floor exercise. The authors warned that many studies were small and at risk of bias, so this is encouraging rather than conclusive. The NHS also notes that pelvic floor exercises can make sex better.

Kegels are not right for everyone, though. If sex is painful or your pelvic floor feels tight, more squeezing can make things worse; relaxation and down-training come first. [Weak vs Tight Pelvic Floor](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/weak-vs-tight-pelvic-floor-women/) explains the difference.

## When to See a Doctor

Book an appointment with your GP, midwife, OB-GYN or a pelvic health physiotherapist if you have:

- Pain during sex that does not ease, or pain at a scar.
- A feeling of heaviness, dragging or a bulge in the vagina, which can be a sign of prolapse.
- Leaking urine, wind or stool.
- Numbness that is getting worse rather than better.
- Bleeding after sex, unusual discharge or signs of infection.
- Low mood, anxiety or loss of interest that lasts more than a couple of weeks.

## Follow a Routine With Guided Timing

Gentle, regular practice matters more than intensity. Kegel Morse Hero is a pelvic floor trainer for everyone, women and men alike: it turns squeezes and rests into Morse-code rhythms, with a dot for a quick squeeze, a dash for a longer hold and gaps for full relaxation, plus haptic cues and slow speeds for beginners. It guides timing only; it does not measure muscle activity or replace postnatal care.

[Explore Kegel Morse Hero on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kegel-morse-hero-pelvic-floor/id6761460873)

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why is there less feeling during sex after a baby?

Usually a mix of a stretched or weaker pelvic floor, healing tears or scars, low estrogen and dryness while breastfeeding, and tiredness or low mood. Most of these improve with time and the right support.

### How long does loss of sensation during sex after birth last?

It varies. Many women notice gradual improvement over the first months as tissue heals and hormones settle. If there is no improvement after several months, ask for a pelvic floor assessment.

### Will sensation come back after breastfeeding?

Dryness linked to low estrogen often eases when breastfeeding reduces or stops and periods return. Lubricant helps in the meantime, and a doctor can discuss other options if dryness persists.

### Should I do Kegels if sex hurts after birth?

Not without assessment. Pain can mean healing problems or an over-tight pelvic floor, which needs relaxation rather than extra squeezing.

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. If sex is painful, you notice bulging or leaking, or your mood is low, see your doctor, midwife or a pelvic floor physical therapist.*

## Less Sensation During Sex in Perimenopause: What Helps
URL: https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/less-sensation-during-sex-perimenopause/
Last reviewed: 2026-11-23

Less feeling during sex and perimenopause often go together. As estrogen falls, vaginal and vulval tissue can become thinner, drier and less well supplied with blood, and arousal can take longer to build. Treatments a doctor can discuss, such as vaginal estrogen, plus lubricants, moisturisers and pelvic floor training, help many women feel more again.

> **Short answer:** Reduced sensation in perimenopause is usually linked to lower estrogen (genitourinary syndrome of menopause), reduced blood flow and sometimes a weak or tense pelvic floor. It is treatable, and it tends not to improve on its own, so it is worth raising with a doctor.

## Less Feeling During Sex and Perimenopause: What's the Link?

Perimenopause is the transition before periods stop, often lasting several years. The NHS lists vaginal dryness, discomfort, painful sex and reduced sex drive among symptoms of both perimenopause and menopause. Many women notice these changes before their periods have actually ended, which is why they can be confusing.

### Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (GSM)

GSM is the medical name for the changes lower estrogen causes in the vulva, vagina and bladder. Clinical references describe:

- Thinner, less elastic vaginal lining.
- Reduced natural lubrication, burning or irritation.
- Changes to the clitoris and vaginal opening.
- Reduced blood flow and slower nerve signals in the area.
- Urinary urgency, frequency or repeated infections.

Each of these can dull sensation directly, or make sex uncomfortable enough that it is hard to relax into pleasure. Unlike hot flushes, GSM symptoms are usually chronic and rarely improve without treatment.

### Blood flow and arousal

Genital sensation depends on blood flow. During arousal, the clitoris and vaginal tissue swell and become more sensitive. With lower estrogen, that response can be slower and weaker, so you may need more time and more direct stimulation to feel the same.

### The pelvic floor

The pelvic floor muscles surround the vagina and contract during orgasm. Weak muscles can mean weaker sensations and orgasms; muscles that are too tight, often after painful sex, can cause pain and make pleasure harder to reach. Both patterns are common in midlife, and they need different approaches. [Weak vs Tight Pelvic Floor](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/weak-vs-tight-pelvic-floor-women/) explains how to tell them apart.

### Other factors

Sleep disruption, stress, mood changes, relationship strain, and medicines such as some antidepressants can all reduce desire and sensation. Conditions like diabetes can also affect nerves and blood flow.

## Treatments a Doctor Can Discuss

| Option | What it does | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Lubricant | Reduces friction during sex | Water- or silicone-based; avoid perfumed products |
| Vaginal moisturiser | Rehydrates tissue over time | Used regularly, often 2–3 times a week, not just before sex |
| Low-dose vaginal estrogen | Restores tissue thickness, moisture and blood flow locally | Prescription; cream, tablet, pessary or ring |
| Vaginal DHEA (prasterone) or ospemifene | Alternatives for persistent symptoms | Prescription; suitability depends on your history |
| Systemic HRT | Treats wider perimenopause symptoms | Prescription; discuss benefits and risks |
| Pelvic floor physiotherapy | Strengthens or relaxes the muscles as needed | Especially if you also leak or have pain |

Clinical guidance suggests starting with moisturisers and lubricants for mild symptoms, and considering low-dose vaginal estrogen or other prescription options when symptoms persist. Because GSM is ongoing, symptoms often return if treatment stops. If you have had breast cancer or another hormone-sensitive condition, talk to your specialist before using any hormonal product.

## Can Pelvic Floor Training Help?

It may help some women, as part of a wider plan. Pelvic floor exercises support bladder control, which often weakens in midlife, and stronger, better-coordinated muscles may contribute to arousal and orgasm. Research specifically in perimenopause is limited, so treat it as a useful addition, not a replacement for treating dryness and tissue changes.

A simple starting routine:

1. Sit or lie comfortably and breathe out.
2. Gently close and lift around the vagina and anus, as if stopping wind and urine.
3. Hold for 3–5 seconds, then release completely for the same time.
4. Repeat 8–10 times, then do a few quick 1-second squeezes.
5. Practise once or twice a day and build slowly over weeks.

If squeezing hurts or sex is painful, start with relaxation instead and see a pelvic health physiotherapist. More age-specific guidance is in [Kegels for Women Over 50 and Menopause](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegels-for-women-over-50-menopause/) and the technique basics in [Kegel Exercises for Women](https://kegelmorsehero.com/articles/kegel-exercises-for-women/).

## When to See a Doctor

Book an appointment if:

- Sex is painful, or dryness has lasted a few weeks despite self-care.
- You have bleeding after sex, between periods or after menopause.
- You notice unusual discharge, itching or burning.
- You feel heaviness, dragging or a bulge in the vagina.
- You leak urine or have repeated urine infections.
- Numbness is getting worse, or came on suddenly.

## Keep a Routine With Guided Timing

Kegel Morse Hero is a pelvic floor trainer for everyone, women and men alike. It turns squeezes and rests into Morse-code rhythms: a dot is a quick squeeze, a dash is a longer hold and the gaps are full relaxation, with haptic cues and reminders. It guides timing only; it does not measure muscle activity or treat menopause symptoms.

[Explore Kegel Morse Hero on the App Store](https://apps.apple.com/us/app/kegel-morse-hero-pelvic-floor/id6761460873)

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Why do I have less sensation during sex in perimenopause?

Falling estrogen can thin and dry vaginal tissue and reduce blood flow, so arousal is slower and sensation weaker. Pelvic floor changes, stress, sleep and some medicines can add to it.

### Does vaginal estrogen help with sensation?

For many women it improves tissue thickness, moisture and comfort, which can make sex more pleasurable. Ask a doctor whether it suits you.

### Can Kegels increase sensitivity in perimenopause?

They may help arousal and orgasm for some women, but they do not fix dryness or thinning tissue. They work best alongside treatment for GSM.

### Will it get better on its own?

GSM symptoms usually do not improve without treatment and may slowly worsen, so it is worth getting help early.

*This article is for general education and is not medical advice. For painful sex, bleeding or ongoing symptoms, see your doctor, a menopause specialist or a pelvic floor physical therapist.*
